I.       INTRODUCTION

         In the Order, the Commission found that PJM’s Tariff “is unjust and unreasonable

because it does not contain provisions addressing with sufficient clarity or consistency the rates,

terms, and conditions of service that apply to generators serving Co-Located Load and Eligible

Customers taking transmission service on behalf of Co-Located Load.”3 Specifically, the

Commission found PJM’s Tariff “unjust and unreasonable because it does not include types of

transmission service that reflect Eligible Customers taking service on behalf of Co-Located

Loads that are willing and able to limit their use of the transmission system under certain

conditions.”4

         The Commission ordered PJM to offer three new forms of transmission service under its

Tariff: (i) Firm Contract Demand transmission service; (ii) Non-Firm Contract Demand

transmission service and (iii) interim, non-firm transmission service.5 The Commission also

established a paper hearing to determine the just and reasonable rates, terms, and conditions for

these new transmission services.6

manifest as follows. First, the rates and terms for the new transmission services must ensure that

Co-Located Load customers11 pay their appropriate share of transmission system costs, including

those related to the benefits of being connected and synchronized with the extensive PJM

Transmission System, which reliably serves 67 million customers. Absent this sharing, existing

ratepayers, including network customers, will be forced to unfairly subsidize Co-Located Load

customers, a result that would be unjust, unreasonable, unduly discriminatory, or preferential.12

        Second, the new transmission services required in the Order must be subject to

appropriate terms and conditions to ensure that the implementation of these new services does

not compromise system reliability. Co-Located Loads, as well as any on-site generators used to

serve those loads, are not islanded. They are fully connected and synchronized with the

transmission system, like all other loads and generators. As such, the full amounts of on-site

identify network upgrades to accommodate transmission service requests for Co-Located Load

beyond those amounts that an Eligible Customer designates for Network Integration

Transmission Service (“NITS”) or Firm Contract Demand Service, the continued reliability of

the system will necessarily depend on the utilization of protection schemes. Thus, these

protection schemes must be subject to comprehensive and rigorous testing and inspection,

 II.     RESPONSES TO PAPER HEARING QUESTIONS

        1. What are the appropriate rates, terms, and conditions for the new Firm Contract
           Demand transmission service, including whether it would be just and reasonable
           to apply the current zonal firm PTPS charges to this new service and whether it
           would be just and reasonable and consistent with cost causation to include charges
           for any of PJM’s administrative services?

        The PJM Transmission Owners propose that the rate for Firm Contract Demand Service

be based on the zonal NITS rates and the underlying NITS revenue requirements. Under this

approach, Eligible Customers taking Firm Contract Demand Service will pay the same base

charge per megawatt (“MW”) as NITS customers, except that unlike NITS customers their

demand will be their specified firm contract demand equal to the firm contract demand amount

(in MWs) multiplied by a single zonal rate for both NITS and Firm Contract Demand Service

customers. Eligible Customers taking Firm Contract Demand Service will also pay a Grid

Reliance Charge for their remaining on-site load, which is not covered by Firm Contract Demand

Service. The design of the Grid Reliance Charge is discussed in response to Question 3 below.

        Additional details regarding the PJM Transmission Owners’ proposal for calculating

Firm Contract Demand Service rates are set forth in the accompanying Direct Joint Testimony of

Peter Blazunas, Lance Schafer, and Hanhan Hammer of Concentric Energy Advisors, Inc.15 As

explained therein, in Zones with formula transmission rates, the single annual rate applicable to

both NITS and Firm Contract Demand Service rates will be established in the same basic manner

as NITS rates are today.16 This rate will be calculated based on each transmission owner’s

annual net revenue requirement, as determined pursuant to the formula rates contained in

        The PJM Transmission Owners are proposing to charge the same rate for Firm Contract

Demand Service and NITS because the level of service provided to both customers is, for all

relevant purposes, the same. Both NITS and Firm Contract Demand Service are firm services

for which network upgrades will be planned and constructed as necessary, with the only

difference being that upgrades for NITS customers are identified based on existing and

anticipated load growth while upgrades for Firm Contract Demand Service customers will be

identified based on their contracted demand level. Firm Contract Demand Service customers

will be able to serve their contracted demand through capacity procured by PJM just like NITS

customers and will not be required to designate specific points of receipt and delivery.

       There is no need or benefit to developing a separate Firm Contract Demand Service rate

or utilizing the existing Firm Point-to-Point Service (“PTPS”) rates.19 Firm PTPS rates are

generally based on the same revenue requirement as the NITS rate, and the nature of Firm

Contract Demand Service, as contemplated in the Order, is essentially a variation of NITS with a

specified contract demand level. Consequently, PJM will need to treat and plan for Firm

Contract Demand Service load in the same manner that it plans for load using NITS, thus

providing service to the Firm Contract Demand Service load on a comparable basis with NITS

load. Because NITS and Firm Contract Demand customers receive comparable benefits, using

the same rate for NITS and Firm Contract Demand Service is consistent with the Commission’s

cost allocation principles, particularly the requirement that transmission customers be allocated

costs roughly commensurate with the estimated benefits they receive.20 On the other hand, it

would be unjust and unreasonable and unduly discriminatory to charge Firm Contract Demand

        Basing the rate for Firm Contract Demand Service on the NITS rate also has the

        2. What are the appropriate rates, terms, and conditions for the new Non-Firm
           Contract Demand transmission service, including whether it would be just and
           reasonable to apply the current zonal non-firm PTPS charges to this new

        The PJM Transmission Owners propose that Non-Firm Contract Demand Service

customers pay a charge for their as-reserved contract demand amount (in MWs) multiplied by a

zonal Non-Firm Contract Demand Service rate determined based on the specific term of service.

The PJM Transmission Owners propose to use the same Firm Contract Demand Service rate for

purposes of establishing the maximum rate for Non-Firm Contract Demand Service. Eligible

Customers taking Non-Firm Contract Demand Service will also pay a Grid Reliance Charge for

their on-site load that is not covered by Firm Contract Demand Service. However, in order to

protect against double-charging Non-Firm Contract Demand Service customers, the Grid

Reliance Charge will be subtracted from the Non-Firm Contract Demand Service charge on a

MWh basis for each MWh of Non-Firm Contract Demand Service included in a transmission

service reservation request.

        Non-Firm Contract Demand Service customers will take service and pay for their

reserved amount of demand based on system availability, and Non-Firm Contract Demand

Service will be available for terms ranging from one hour to one month.24 As discussed in the

Blazunas, Schafer, and Hammer Direct Joint Testimony, in other respects the Non-Firm Contract

Demand Service rate will be computed in the same manner as the Firm Contract Demand Service

          3. As noted above, a Co-Location Arrangement is synchronized to the transmission
            system. Should the rate paid by an Eligible Customer on behalf of a Co-Located
            load taking only the new Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service that
            elects to not reserve any amount of that service for a period of time (e.g., one
            month) reflect not only charges for regulation and black start services, but also an
            additional charge given that regulation and black start services could not be
            provided without the transmission system? If so, how should that additional
            charge be determined?

         The PJM Transmission Owners are proposing to charge a Grid Reliance Charge to

Eligible Customers taking the new Contract Demand services based on the difference between

the amount of their firm contract demand for Firm Contract Demand Service or, in the case of

Non-Firm Contract Demand Service customers, the amount of their reserved service, and their

total (gross) on-site load.34 The proposed Grid Reliance Charge is designed to reflect the costs of

using the transmission system to deliver black start and regulation services, as well as providing

the inherent benefits that all customers, including Contract Demand customers, receive as a

result of their synchronization to and reliance on the grid.35 The Grid Reliance Charge also

recognizes the costs associated with the operations, maintenance, and other activities that PJM

Transmission Owners will need to perform for the grid and to accommodate the increased

number of protection schemes that will be required for Co-Located Load customers. As

discussed further below, and in the Blazunas, Schafer, and Hammer Direct Joint Testimony, the

PJM Transmission Owners initially propose to calculate this charge for each zone based on an

average fixed percentage of the portion of transmission depreciation and operations and

maintenance (“O&M”) expense associated with providing grid reliance services, and then

applying that percentage to each PJM Transmission Owner’s Attachment H annual transmission

          Compensation for providing black start and regulation services, as distinct from delivery of those services,
will be received by the providers of those services.

 revenue requirement.36 The initial percentage is 25.8 percent, subject to adjustment every five

years as discussed below.

         As Commissioner Chang stated in her concurrence to the Order, a minimum charge such

as the Grid Reliance Charge is “particularly essential to protecting customers against

transmission cost shifts under the new framework established through [the Order].”37

Commissioner Chang went on to explain that all Co-Located Loads are synchronized with the

grid through their generators, and rely on the PJM grid.38 The PJM Transmission Owners agree.

The Grid Reliance Charge is necessary and appropriate to ensure that Co-Located Load

customers pay their appropriate share of transmission system costs. Co-Located Load and its

associated generation is electrically connected to the transmission system (not islanded) and

therefore benefits from the existence and reliable operation of the transmission system and

should contribute to paying the costs of continuing to reliably operate the system regardless of

the amount of energy withdrawn. Even with a zero MW contract demand, a large Co‑Located

Load and generation arrangement will still depend on the grid for the delivery of various

ancillary services and a suite of synchronization support services, such as stable frequency,

inertia, stability services (damping, angle stability), fault current capability, and ride-through and

protection coordination. In short, a Co-Located Load’s net withdrawals do not fully reflect its

actual reliance on the grid.

         Although the proliferation of large Co-Located Load arrangements is a relatively recent

phenomenon, the Commission has long recognized that an integrated transmission system


36
         As noted above, a handful of PJM transmission owners continue to utilize stated rates, which in some cases
are based on black-box settlements and may need to be accounted for in specific stated rates for the new firm and non-
firm contract demand services. This also applies to the Grid Reliance Charge.
37
         Order, Chang, Comm’r, concurring at P 5.
38
         Id. at P 6.



                                                         15
 provides broad reliability benefits to all customers of the system.39 This recognition has guided

Commission decisions relating to issues such as ratemaking and cost allocations.40 Consistent

with this longstanding policy, as well as cost allocation rules,41 it is appropriate to require Co-

Located Load customers to pay their appropriate share of costs of relying on the system to

deliver necessary ancillary services and grid support to reliably connect their on-site load and

generation.

        The Grid Reliance Charge methodology proposed by the PJM Transmission Owners

represents a just and reasonable means of estimating the grid reliance benefits to Co-Located

Load with an appropriate level of precision, while ensuring that the Grid Reliance Charge can be

fairly and efficiently implemented.42 Pursuant to this methodology, the Grid Reliance Charge

will be determined on an annual basis by multiplying an average fixed percentage of the portion

of transmission costs associated with providing grid reliance services by each PJM Transmission

Owner’s Attachment H annual transmission revenue requirement. Using annual depreciation and

O&M expenses to establish the Grid Reliance Charge is appropriate because these expenses best

capture the portions of a transmission owner’s revenue requirement relating to the ongoing

reliable operation of the grid.

        A detailed discussion of the methodology for calculating the Grid Reliance Charge is set

forth in the Blazunas, Schafer, and Hammer Direct Joint Testimony.43 As explained by Mr.

Schafer, the fixed percentage allocator is based on costs included in transmission plant and

(1988)); see also Order No. 1000 and Order No. 1920.

Transmission Owners, that provide grid reliance capability.44 Mr. Schafer adopted a

conservative approach in a number of respects, such as by excluding amortization and general

plant depreciation, as well as administrative and general (A&G) expenses.45 The allocator will

be multiplied by each PJM Transmission Owner’s rate for NITS and Firm Contract Demand

Service to arrive at an “unadjusted” Grid Reliance Charge rate. This unadjusted rate will then be

multiplied by a ratio that accounts for the difference between the demand used to account for the

NITS and Firm Contract Demand Service rate (NITS customer load plus Firm Contract Demand

Service load) and Co-Located Load customers’ gross load, to arrive at the final Grid Reliance

Charge for each Zone.46

       The Grid Reliance Charge will be calculated on a zonal basis, as opposed to a blended,

PJM-wide basis. Because black start service is procured zonally, delivery obligations are

inherently local. Likewise, most synchronization support is provided at the local rather than

regional level. These factors support calculating the Grid Reliance Charge on a zone-by-zone

basis, just like the Firm Contract Demand Service and Non-Firm Contract Demand Service rates.

       The PJM Transmission Owners also propose to recalculate and update the allocation

percentages used to establish the Grid Reliance Charge every five years, using the same

averaging approach. This will ensure a reasonable level of year-to-year rate stability while

ensuring that the allocators do not become overly stale over time.

       Finally, the PJM Transmission Owners propose to treat the revenues from the Grid

Reliance Charge by applying them as a dollar-for-dollar credit to NITS and Firm Contract

 Demand Service customers located in the relevant Zone based on their share of the coincident

peak load. This will ensure that the Grid Reliance Charge does not result in a double recovery

for the PJM Transmission Owners or inappropriate cost shifts.

set forth in the Blazunas, Schafer and Hammer Direct Joint Testimony.47 However, a simplified

example showing the determination and application of the Grid Reliance Charge is set forth

        5. What is the appropriate penalty charge or other remedial action that PJM should
          take to address any unreserved use of the PJM transmission system for an Eligible
          Customer taking Firm Contract Demand transmission service on behalf of a Co-
          Located load?

       Robust penalty provisions are a necessary component of the new services required by the

Commission. First, and most importantly, any penalties must be sufficient to meaningfully deter

Co-Located Load customers from exceeding their contract demand and making unreserved use

of the transmission system. Because network upgrades are planned and built only to

accommodate load covered by Firm Contract Demand Service or NITS, it is of the utmost

importance that Co-Located Loads respect their contractual limits, including any related

curtailment or other instructions from PJM. This concern is particularly acute because many of

these arrangements will likely involve substantial amounts of load—hundreds, if not thousands

of MWs—being served by on-site generation but still connected to the grid. If these limits are

not respected, the reliability consequences to the system could be severe. Therefore, operational

penalties must be structured to meaningfully deter load customers that exceed reserved service

amounts. Financial penalties alone are insufficient.

       The PJM Transmission Owners understand that PJM intends to propose operational

penalties, and agree with PJM that the imposition of such penalties is appropriate. The PJM

Transmission Owners believe that any penalty regime should rely on both operational

consequences and complementary financial penalties. The PJM Transmission Owners

understand that, at a high level, PJM’s proposal would be to refer to FERC enforcement or

applicable reliability organizations any failure to comply with PJM operating instructions. In

addition, PJM is proposing a “two-strike” approach, pursuant to which if a customer’s protective

systems fail to operate as required, PJM would first determine whether to impose a 120-day

“pause” in service and, with the second failure, would terminate the customer’s Contract



                                               19
 Demand Service contract and the customer would be required to become a NITS customer if it

wished to resume service. The PJM Transmission Owners believe this proposal is a good

starting point conceptually, but recognize that additional details will need to be developed as to

how these operational consequences would be applied. As such, the PJM Transmission Owners

reserve the right to provide further input as part of this paper hearing process when further

information becomes available.

       The PJM Transmission Owners also believe that a financial penalty structure is

appropriate to complement and supplement operational penalties implemented by PJM.

Although the PJM Transmission Owners anticipate that operational penalties will provide a

significant deterrent against Co-Located Load customers exceeding their reserved transmission

service use, financial penalties could still play a valuable role in enhancing this deterrent as well

as ensuring the market and other ratepayers are made whole if a Co-Located Load customer

exceeds its contract demand. In addition, it may also be appropriate to impose financial penalties

when a Co-Located Load customer deviates from its contract demand even if such deviations are

mitigated by a Special Protection Scheme (“SPS”) or Remedial Action Scheme (“RAS”)

installed on the Transmission Owner side of the point of interconnection. The PJM

Transmission Owners intend to work with PJM in continuing to explore the penalty options and

will, if appropriate, offer a proposal at a subsequent stage of this paper hearing process.

       6. What is the appropriate penalty charge or other remedial action that PJM should
          take to address any unreserved use of the PJM transmission system for an Eligible
          Customer taking Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service on behalf of a
          Co-Located load?

       See response to Question 5.




                                                 20
         7. What are the appropriate mechanisms for an anti-toggling feature for the Firm
           Contract Demand transmission service, including the appropriate minimum
           service period and minimum notice period for discontinuing or modifying the
           level of service?

        The Order indicates that Firm Contract Demand Service should have a minimum term of

one year. However, as the Commission recognized, there are concerns regarding a customer’s

ability to toggle between firm and non-firm service levels.49 One of the primary concerns with

permitting Firm Contract Demand Service customers to take service for a single-year term is that

PJM will be required to procure capacity for these customers, and one-year commitments will

not encourage the appropriate price signals necessary to incent additional needed capacity.

There also is a potential concern that Firm Contract Demand Service customers will cause the

need for network upgrades to accommodate their Firm Contract Demand Service and then exit

the system, thereby potentially shifting costs to other customers.50 To partially address these

concerns, the PJM Transmission Owners propose a five-year minimum commitment period for

Firm Contract Demand Service. A five-year minimum commitment period is appropriate

because, as noted by the Commission in the Order, it mirrors the commitment period for loads

seeking to procure their own capacity.51

        With respect to minimum notice obligations, the PJM Transmission Owners recommend

the Commission adopt the same requirements for Firm Contract Demand Service that currently

apply to notices of termination for NITS under Section 2.5 of the PJM Tariff.52 This is


49
        Order at P 213.
50
         Id. at P 213. If network upgrades are attributable to the Firm Contract Demand Service, these may require
separate payment guarantees to prevent NITS customers from being left “holding the bag” if a Firm Contract Demand
Service customer leaves before the costs of the upgrades are fully paid.
51
         Id. (“PJM’s capacity market includes anti-toggling measures, including the ‘must offer’ requirement for
existing Capacity Resources and the five-year minimum commitment for loads seeking to procure their own capacity
through the Fixed Resource Requirement alternative.”).
52
         PJM Tariff, Section 2.5 (“Although Regional Network Integration Service is presumed to continue without
expiration, it may be terminated where:


                                                       21
 appropriate given the concerns regarding toggling and the resulting potential for cost shifting

discussed above.

       8. What interconnection requirements and operational practices are necessary for
          special protection schemes to maintain system reliability (e.g., the need for full
          redundancy of such schemes) in the event that a Co-Located load itself or its
          associated generator trips offline?

       The PJM Transmission Owners are not offering a specific proposal at this time relating to

these issues, but highlight a number of concerns and key elements relating to interconnection,

planning and operational practices for Co-Located Load customers taking Firm Contract

Demand Service, Non-Firm Contract Demand Service, or interim, non-firm transmission service.

       Significant ink has been spilled already in this proceeding regarding the appropriateness

of relying on protection schemes such as RAS in lieu of requiring Co-Located Load customers to

take NITS for their full on-site load. The PJM Transmission Owners will not repeat those

arguments here. However, there are certain key facts that the Commission should take into

consideration in order to allow the new transmission services to be implemented in a safe and

reliable manner. Without network upgrades being planned to serve the entire amount of a

customer’s on-site load, the reliability of the PJM system will necessarily depend on the

adequate deployment and effective operation of SPS or RAS to ensure that Co-Located Load

customers respect their contractual limitations. This will result in the PJM system relying on




       1) An incumbent Network Customer will be replaced by a successor Network Customer, in which case the
          incumbent’s service shall only terminate if the successor agrees to commence the taking of service, the
          appropriate service agreement is executed, and all other applicable terms and conditions of the PJM
          Governing Agreements are satisfied;
       2) An incumbent Network Customer seeks to terminate its service and no successor Network Customer
          exists, in which case the incumbent must provide PJM with forty-two (42) months’ notice prior to the
          commencement of a Delivery Year, subject to receiving all necessary regulatory approvals for such
          termination, if any; or
       3) On such other date mutually agreed upon by the parties.”).


                                                      22
 SPS or RAS, potentially including customer-operated systems, to secure reliable operations.53

Although SPS/RAS are already employed in PJM, the use of multiple SPS/RAS to protect the

grid from large amounts of on-site load exceeding their contractual withdrawal limitations rather

than more permanent solutions is novel. To address issues arising from this novel approach, the

PJM Transmission Owners suggest the following:

           The Commission should adopt rigorous and comprehensive requirements to ensure

            that this novel reliance on SPS/RAS does not result in adverse reliability impacts,

            including potential violations of North American Electric Reliability Corporation

            (“NERC”) criteria. To that end, the PJM Transmission Owners recommend the

            following: All SPS and RAS should be fully redundant. Although failures of

            protection schemes are relatively rare, they do occur, and given the large amount of

            on-site load and generation potentially involved in these arrangements, it is crucially

            important to protect against such failures.

           The Commission should require the Co-Located Load customer to pay for PJM and

            PJM Transmission Owner-administered studies to ensure any SPS or RAS can

            effectively mitigate the risks of potential failure modes.

           The PJM Transmission Owners should have the option to review and agree to any

            customer load curtailment procedures or operational control mechanisms.

           All SPS and RAS must fully meet PJM and PJM Transmission Owner technical criteria.

           The Commission should consider requiring more frequent testing of SPS and RAS

            than is currently required by NERC Reliability Standards, with particular attention to




53
       Examples of potential approaches as to how these SPS/RAS might be implemented are discussed in the
accompanying testimony. See Blazunas, Schafer and Hammer Direct Joint Testimony at 39.


                                                   23
             protection equipment installed on the customer side of the point of interconnection.

            Results from tests of customer-side protection schemes should be submitted to both

            PJM and the interconnected PJM Transmission Owner, and any SPS or RAS found to

            be inadequate/insufficient should be updated accordingly.

           The Commission should permit PJM and the PJM Transmission Owners to

            implement and enforce reasonable limits on the total amount of load that can be

            covered by SPS or RAS, particularly for customers in relatively close proximity to

            one another or in a transmission-constrained area.

           The Commission should permit PJM Transmission Owners the option to require the

            implementation of SPS or RAS on the Transmission Owner’s side of the point of

            interconnection and to require that the costs associated with such SPS or RAS be fully

            recoverable.

           The Commission should permit the PJM Transmission Owners to exercise an option

            to own, maintain, and operate any SPS or RAS installed on the customer’s side of the

            point of interconnection, at the customer’s expense.

           The Commission should direct NERC to establish requirements that Co-Located Load

            customers register with NERC so that those customers may be responsible for

            meeting NERC’s reliability standards, including NERC Reliability Standard PRC-

            012-2.

        Additionally, the Commission must strictly enforce compliance with NERC Reliability

Standard PRC-012-2, which includes nine requirements to address all aspects of RAS.54 The

PJM Transmission Owners emphasize particularly the importance of requirements 3, 4, and 8 of


54
         North American Electric Reliability Corporation, PRC-012-2 – Remedial Action Schemes (June 12, 2025),
https://www.nerc.com/globalassets/standards/reliability-standards/prc/prc-012-2.pdf.


                                                     24
 PRC-012-2. Requirement R3 outlines the RAS component of Dependability, which is a measure

of certainty of a device to operate when required. For instance, if a RAS is installed to meet

system performance requirements, the RAS’s failure to operate when intended would put the

system at risk. This risk can be mitigated by designing the RAS so that it will accomplish its

intended purpose while experiencing a single RAS component failure. Such a design is typically

achieved through redundancy. Other strategies include “over-tripping” load or generation, or

alternative backup schemes. Requirement R4 of PRC-012-2 requires the reliability planning

coordinator to perform a periodic evaluation of each RAS within its planning area, at least once

every five years. These evaluations must determine whether each RAS: (1) mitigates the system

conditions or contingencies for which it was designated; and (2) avoids adverse interactions with

other RAS and special protection systems. The Commission must ensure that any new

requirements or flexibility provided to Co-Located Load customers do not hinder the planning

coordinator’s ability to complete these evaluations and comply with the reliability standards

devised to protect the system from catastrophic failure. Similarly, Requirement R8 of PRC-012-

2 requires periodic testing of RAS performance, i.e., every six years for normal RAS and every

12 years for limited impact RAS. The Commission should consider whether more frequent

testing is advisable, particularly for protection installed on the customer side of the point of

interconnection.

       With respect to interconnection requirements, the PJM Transmission Owners emphasize

that they will still need to perform load integration studies for any Co-Located Load

arrangements, just as they do today with respect to any large load customers. These studies

could involve some or all of the following analyses: (i) what, if any, upgrades are needed to

accommodate the physical gross load amount behind the point of interconnection; (ii) the request




                                                 25
 for firm contract demand amount in front of the point of interconnection; (iii) the impacts that

would result from additional load located on-site (behind the point of interconnection) but being

served by on-site (behind the point of interconnection) generation and how those impacts need to

be addressed, including appropriate protection schemes; and (iv) what additional measures are

necessary to accommodate non-firm contract demand service requests in front of the point of

interconnection.

III.   CONCLUSION

       The PJM Transmission Owners appreciate the opportunity to submit their initial

responses to the paper hearing questions posed by the Commission in the Order. The PJM

Transmission Owners respectfully request that any subsequent Commission orders addressing

these issues adopt the proposals and recommendations set forth herein.

 2   Q.   What are NERC’s transmission planning standards and why is transmission owner

 3        and transmission provider compliance with those standards important?

 4   A.   [Hammer] The North American Electric Reliability Corporation’s (“NERC”)

 5        Transmission Planning (“TPL”) standards establish mandatory planning requirements to

 6        ensure the Bulk Electric System can reliably withstand credible contingencies over

 7        planning horizons. TPL-001 Transmission System Planning Performance Requirements is

 8        the foundational and currently enforceable transmission planning standard. Its purpose is

 9        to ensure that the Bulk Electric System is planned so it will operate reliably across a broad

10        range of system conditions and contingencies, from normal conditions to extreme events.

11               Compliance with the NERC TPL-001 requirements is important because they

12        ensure the transmission system is planned to reliably withstand credible outages and system

13        stresses, reducing the risk of cascading failures and large-scale blackouts. For transmission

14        owners and providers, TPL-001 compliance also minimizes regulatory and financial risk,

15        supports coordinated regional planning, and provides a defensible technical basis for

16        transmission investments needed to maintain long-term grid reliability.

17   Q.   Does the Order’s proposal to rely on SPS/RAS to accommodate Co-Located Load

18        transmission service requests present any reliability or planning concerns?

19   A.   [Hammer] Yes. Under the principle of TPL-001, transmission planners must plan for load

20        that has the ability to draw power from the transmission system, not merely for load that is

21        expected or intended to do so under normal operating conditions. Reliance on SPS/RAS as

22        a substitute for timely network upgrades raises significant concerns under established good

23        utility practices and applicable NERC reliability standards. SPS/RAS are generally
                                                                             Exhibit No. PTO-0001
                                                                                     Page 34 of 39

 1        intended as supplemental or last-resort reliability measures, not a primary tool to

 2        accommodate incremental transmission services on a routine or ongoing basis. In

 3        particular, substituting SPS/RAS for network upgrade identification, design, coordination,

 4        testing, and commissioning risks undermining the transparency and predictability of the

 5        transmission planning process. Transmission Owners must ensure that all applicable

 6        performance requirements under NERC Standard TPL‑001 remain satisfied, including

 7        under stressed system conditions and under reasonable worst‑case assumptions such as

 8        SPS/RAS failure, mis-operation, or unavailability.

 9               Accordingly, any planning assumptions that rely on SPS/RAS must demonstrate

10        acceptable system performance both with and without successful SPS/RAS operation.

11        Absent such demonstrations, reliance on SPS/RAS to accommodate Co‑Located Load

12        transmission service requests could defer necessary upgrades, increase operational risk,

13        and impede prudent transmission planning and reliable operation of the Bulk Electric

14        System.

15   Q.   Are there any other grid challenges associated with utilizing SPS/RAS to ensure

16        reliability in connection with Co-Located Load taking contract demand transmission

17        service?

18   A.   [Hammer] Yes. SPS/RAS are operational tools rather than transmission facilities. While

19        they can be effective when properly designed and operated, they introduce dependencies

20        related to system protection performance, communications, and coordination during

21        stressed system conditions. Individual SPS/RAS-backed Firm Contract Demand Service

22        requests may appear manageable in isolation; however, the cumulative impact of multiple

23        large Firm Contract Demand Service loads relying on SPS/RAS – particularly within the

 6        stakeholders should understand when infrastructure investment becomes necessary

16        contract demand transmission services are addressed through both primary,

17        customer‑owned protection and an optional, transmission‑owner‑owned backstop, rather

18        than reliance on a single protection scheme.

19                Under this framework, the primary responsibility for limiting withdrawals from the

20        transmission system remains with the interconnection customer or Co‑Located Load,

21        typically through customer-owned SPS/RAS that are designed, operated, and maintained

22        in accordance with applicable NERC standards and reviewed by PJM. To help accomplish

23        this, the Commission should direct NERC to establish requirements that Co-Located Load
                                                                              Exhibit No. PTO-0001
                                                                                      Page 37 of 39

 1        Customers register with NERC so that those customers may be responsible for meeting

 2        NERC’s reliability standards. These customer‑owned schemes serve as the first line of

 3        defense and are expected to operate under normal and reasonably foreseeable contingency

 4        conditions.

 5               “Full redundancy” does not mean duplicative or parallel protection for every

 6        contingency, nor does it imply that transmission owners must install SPS/RAS in all cases.

 7        Rather, it means that, where system studies identify elevated reliability risk, transmission

 8        owners should have the option to implement a transmission-owner-owned SPS/RAS as a

 9        secondary backstop to protect the Bulk Electric System in the event of customer‑owned

10        scheme failure, mis-operation, or unavailability.

11   Q.   How does this concept of redundancy align with NERC reliability standards,

12        including PRC-012?

13   A.   [Hammer] This approach is fully consistent with NERC Reliability Standard PRC‑012,

14        which expressly contemplates that SPS/RAS may be owned by Transmission Owners,

15        Generator Owners, or Distribution Providers, provided that ownership and accountability

16        are clearly defined. Importantly, PRC‑012 does not prohibit multiple SPS/RAS acting on

17        the same system condition, nor does it require exclusive reliance on a single owner’s

18        protection scheme. Allowing a Transmission Owner to own and operate a backstop

19        SPS/RAS therefore fits within the PRC‑012 framework.

20   Q.   Why is reliance on a single, customer‑owned SPS/RAS insufficient in some cases?

21   A.   [Hammer] Transmission planning and operating standards, including TPL‑001, require

22        planners to account for credible contingencies and protection system failures, including

23        single points of failure and mis-operations. In configurations where Co‑Located Load
                                                                               Exhibit No. PTO-0001
                                                                                       Page 38 of 39

 1        depends on SPS/RAS to limit transmission system withdrawals, exclusive reliance on a

 2        single, customer‑controlled protection scheme can introduce reliability risk, particularly if

 3        the equipment is unavailable due to outage or maintenance. In high‑impact scenarios,

 4        failure of the primary SPS/RAS could result in unexpected load appearing on the

 5        transmission system, potentially leading to overloads, stability concerns, or emergency

 6        operating actions. A transmission-owner‑owned backstop SPS/RAS provides an additional

 7        layer of assurance that these risks can be mitigated before they affect other transmission

 8        customers or system reliability.

 9   Q.   Does “full redundancy” shift responsibility or cost from customers to Transmission

10        Owners?

11   A.   [Hammer] No. The concept of full redundancy does not shift responsibility away from

12        customers. The presence of a transmission-owner‑owned backstop does not relieve

13        customers of compliance obligations, nor does it entitle customers to rely on transmission-

14        owner‑owned protection in lieu of their own facilities.

15   Q.   Why is the ability to selectively curtail load essential to the contract demand

16        transmission service framework adopted by the Commission, and how is that

17        capability implemented in practice at the point of interconnection?

18   A.   [Hammer] The Commission directed PJM to create contract demand transmission service

19        to reflect loads that are willing and able to limit their withdrawals from the transmission

20        system. Load taking contract demand transmission service is granted access to the

21        transmission system without corresponding reliability reinforcements to support the full

22        gross load, therefore, the reliability condition is curtailment.
                                                                                Exhibit No. PTO-0001
                                                                                        Page 39 of 39

 1               Under certain system conditions, PJM and the PJM Transmission Owners have the

 2        authority to shed the non‑firm portion of load, either preemptively or immediately

 3        following a contingency. For example, PJM may arm a SPS/RAS to instantaneously drop

 4        a large block of load upon the trip of the on-site generator, thereby preventing a thermal or

 5        stability overload.

 6               Where a point of interconnection serves both firm and non‑firm contract demand,

 7        the interconnection must be designed to allow selective curtailment. Operationally, this

 8        typically requires that firm and non‑firm load be served through separate breakers, feeders,

 9        or other independently controllable facilities. The Transmission Owner may structure the

10        interconnection so that the non‑firm portion can be shed without interrupting firm service.

11               Examples could include:

12           Separate feeder lines or breakers dedicated to firm versus non‑firm load;

13           Partial load‑shedding schemes that trip only designated non‑firm MW; or

14           For large facilities such as data centers, multiple transformer banks, with some

15            designated as “firm service” and others as “non‑firm service,” allowing independent

16            tripping.

17               Critically, the ability to distinguish and shed the non‑firm portion of load

18        independently is a prerequisite for a contract demand service model. Curtailment cannot

19        be all‑or‑nothing; the firm portion of load is expected to remain in service except under

20        last‑resort system conditions. As a result, compliance may require the installation of special

21        protection or control equipment at the substation or within the customer’s facilities.

22   Q.   Does this complete your testimony at this time?

23   A.   [Blazunas, Schafer, and Hammer] Yes.
